exercise.title: Why is the derivative the multiplier of a small input change?

statement.p: Local linear approximation says \Delta y\approx f'(a)\Delta x. In your own words, why does that make f'(a) a converter from a small input error into a small output error, and why is this the practical meaning of the derivative in measurement?

hint.p: The tangent line is the first model of how output responds to input. Differentials are the same idea written as dy=f'(x)\,dx.

subsection.title: Relative and percentage error
subsection.p: Absolute error tells the size of the error in the units of the quantity. Relative error compares the error to the size of the quantity itself.

paragraphs.title: Power laws
paragraphs.p: where C\neq0 and n are constants, and x>0. Then
For a power law, the magnitude of the relative output error is approximately |n| times the magnitude of the relative input error.
This is why small measurement errors can grow when a formula contains powers.

exercise.title: Why is relative error a different question from absolute error?

statement.p: Absolute error keeps the units of the quantity. Relative error compares the error to the size of the quantity itself. In your own words, why can a small absolute error still be a large relative error, or the reverse, and why do power laws make relative error especially readable?

hint.p: An error of one centimeter is huge for a bacterium and tiny for a planet. For y=cx^n, relative error in y is about |n| times relative error in x.

subsection.title: Sensitivity in measurement
subsection.p: A large value of |f'(x)| means that a small input error can create a large output error. A small value of |f'(x)| means the output is less sensitive to input error.

exercise.title: Why does a large |f'| mean high sensitivity?

statement.p: The derivative has units of output per input. In your own words, why does a steep graph turn a small measurement error into a large output error, and why might a surveyor’s angle error matter more at some elevations than at others?

hint.p: Sensitivity is |f'(x)|. Where the function is steep, the output is more easily disturbed by input error.

note.p: For y=f(x), the size of |f'(x)| tells how strongly errors in x are amplified into errors in y.

subsection.p: Linear approximation gives us three related calculations:
The input-change estimate requires f\prime(x)\ne0. So far we have mostly used the first and third. The second one is about to become a method for solving equations.
If f(x) is not zero, how far should we move x so that f(x) becomes zero? The tangent line gives the first guess. Repeating that guess gives Newton’s method.
